Apex supports comprehensive table syntax including standard pipe tables, CSV/TSV tables, and advanced features like column/row spans, per-cell alignment, captions, and IAL attributes.

Standard Pipe Tables

Basic pipe table syntax with header row and separator: 

| Header 1 | Header 2 | Header 3 |
| -------- | :------: | -------: |
| Left     |  Center  |    Right |
| Data     |   Data   |     Data |

Column alignment is specified in the separator row:

  • :--- or --- - Left (default)
  • :---: - Center
  • ---: - Right

Relaxed Tables

In unified and kramdown modes, tables don’t require separator rows: 

one | two | three
1 | 2 | 3
4 | 5 | 6

This automatically becomes a table. See Modes for details.

Grid Tables (Pandoc-style)

Pandoc grid tables use ASCII border rows instead of pipe separators. Enable with --grid-tables or disable explicitly with --no-grid-tables (disabled by default in unified mode). 

+---------------+---------------+
| Fruit         | Price         |
+:=============+==============:+
| Bananas       | $1.34         |
| Oranges       | $2.10         |
+---------------+---------------+

Features supported:

  • Header rows (+===+ separator)
  • Column alignment from : markers in border rows (+:===+, +===:+, +:===:+)
  • Multiline cells (including lists and other block markdown in cells)
  • Full-row colspan (single cell spanning the table width)
  • Nested grids inside colspan cells
  • Partial in-row separators (| Label +---+---+ patterns) with rowspan/colspan Notes:
  • Grid tables require a blank line before and after the table block (same as pipe tables).
  • Lines inside fenced code blocks are never converted.
  • Complex layouts may differ slightly from Pandoc; see Limitations and Roadmap.

Headerless Tables

Apex supports tables that start with alignment rows (separator rows) without header rows. The alignment specified in the separator row is automatically applied to all columns: 

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a   | b   | c   |
| 1   | 2   | 3   |

Alignment specifiers work as usual: 

|  |  |  |
|:---|:---:|---:|
| left | center | right |

In this case, the first row (the alignment row) specifies the column alignment, and all subsequent data rows inherit that alignment. The empty header row that would normally be required is automatically handled.

Row Header Columns

You can mark the first column as a row-header column by starting the header row with an empty first cell: 

|   | Header 1 | Header 2 |
| Row 1 | data 1.1 | data 1.2 |
| Row 2 | data 2.1 | data 2.2 |

When the first header cell is empty (for example, | | or | |), Apex will:

  • Treat the rest of the header row as usual column headers.
  • Render the first cell of each body row as a row header using <th scope="row">Row 1</th>, <th scope="row">Row 2</th>, etc. Notes:
  • The row-header behavior only applies to the first column and only when the first header cell is empty.
  • Tables that start with |data|data| or data|data do not enable row headers.
  • This works together with all other table features (relaxed tables, headerless tables, colspans/rowspans, captions, etc.).

Inline Tables from CSV/TSV

In addition to regular pipe tables, Apex can convert inline CSV/TSV text into tables.

Fenced CSV/TSV Tables

Use a fenced code block with the info string table. The delimiter is detected automatically:

  • If any non-blank line contains a tab, the block is treated as TSV.
  • Otherwise, if any non-blank line contains a comma, the block is treated as CSV.
  • If no tabs or commas are found, the block is left unchanged as a normal table-info code block (useful for showing literal CSV/TSV). 
```table
header 1,header 2,header 3
data 1,data 2,data 3
,,data 2c
```

You can also use TSV with real tab characters: 

```table
col1	col2	col3
val1	val2	val3
```

Alignment Rows in CSV/TSV Tables

CSV/TSV inline tables can specify column alignment using a row of alignment keywords: 

```table
H1,H2,H3
left,center,right
a,b,c
```

The alignment row is not rendered as data; it is converted to the equivalent Markdown alignment row:

  • left → :---
  • center → :---:
  • right → ---:
  • auto → --- If the first row contains only alignment keywords, it becomes a headless table: the alignment row is emitted first and all following rows become body rows. If there is no alignment row at all, Apex emits a default --- separator row so that relaxed/headless table handling still works as expected.

<!--TABLE--> Markers

You can also start an inline CSV/TSV table with an HTML comment: 

<!--TABLE-->
header 1,header 2,header 3
data 1,data 2,data 3
,,data 2c
| consumes the following contiguous non-blank lines as table data (stopping at the first blank line) applies the same delimiter detection and optional alignment-row handling and converts the block into a table. If no tabs or commas are found the comment and lines are left unchanged.

Column Spans

Column spans allow a cell to span multiple columns. There are two ways to create column spans:

Consecutive Pipes

Use consecutive pipes with no content between them to create column spans. Place the consecutive pipes after the cell content, and they will cause that cell to span the specified number of additional columns: 

|        | Table  | Has   | Colspans       |
| ------ | ------ | ---   | -------------- |
| row 1                 ||| colspan        |
| row 2  | span 2        || &larr; colspan |
  • | << | (2 consecutive pipes) causes the previous cell to span 2 columns total (its own column plus 1 additional)
  • | << | << | (3 consecutive pipes) causes the previous cell to span 3 columns total (its own column plus 2 additional)
  • | << | << | << | (4 consecutive pipes) causes the previous cell to span 4 columns total (its own column plus 3 additional) In the first row above, | << | << | after “colspan” causes “colspan” to span across 3 columns total. In the second row, | << | after “cell” causes “cell” to span across 2 columns total (its own column plus the next column).

<< Marker

You can also use the << marker in a cell to force a colspan without using consecutive pipes. This allows whitespace and table alignment in the Markdown source: 

| A   | B   | C   |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D   | <<  | <<  |

The << marker creates a column span just like consecutive pipes, but allows you to maintain proper table alignment and add whitespace for readability in your source Markdown. Each << marker in a cell indicates that cell is part of a colspan from the previous cell. In the example above, D spans 3 columns total (its own column plus the 2 columns containing << markers). To include a literal << in a table cell (without creating a colspan), escape the first < with a backslash: \<<. The backslash-plus-less-than is treated as an escaped <, so \<< is rendered as the two characters << and does not trigger colspan behavior. For text plus literal << (e.g. “raw <<”), use raw \<< so the cell is not treated as a colspan and the column is preserved. Note: Blank cells containing whitespace (like | | or | |) are rendered as empty cells, not as column spans. Only cells with no whitespace and no content between consecutive pipes (like | << | or | << | << |) create column spans.

Row Spans

Row spans allow a cell to span multiple rows. Use the ^^ marker to create a row span: 

| A   | B   |
| --- | --- |
| C   | D   |
| ^^  | E   |

The ^^ marker creates a row span on the cell above. In this example, the cell containing “C” spans two rows. Consecutive ^^ markers stack to create larger row spans: 

| A   | B   | C   |
| --- | --- | --- |
| X   | Y   | Z   |
| ^^  | W   | V   |
| ^^  | U   | T   |

Here, the cell “X” spans three rows total.

Combined Row and Column Spans

You can mix rowspans and colspans in the same table to create more complex layouts: 

| Department  | Employee | Q1-Q2 Average | Q3     | Q4  | Overall |
| ----------- | -------- | ------------- | ------ | --- | ------- |
| Engineering | Alice    | 93.5          | 94     | 96  | 94.25   |
| ^^          | Bob      | 89.0          | 87     | 91  | 89.00   |
| Marketing   | Charlie  | 92.0          | Absent |     | 92.00   |
| Sales       | Diana    | 87.5          | 88     | 90  | 88.50   |
| ^^          | Eve      | 93.0          | 95     | 93  | 93.50   |

Here ^^ creates rowspans for the Department column. The example demonstrates how rowspans work with regular data rows.

Individual Cell Alignment

Table cells can be aligned individually using colons, similar to Jekyll Spaceship. This allows you to override the default column alignment on a per-cell basis: 

| Header | Header | Header |
| --- | --- | --- |
| :Left | Center: | :Center: |
| Right: | Normal | :Left |

Alignment syntax:

  • :Text or : Text - Left align (leading colon)
  • Text: or Text : - Right align (trailing colon)
  • :Text: or : Text : - Center align (both colons) The colons are removed from the output, and the alignment is applied via CSS text-align styles. Escaped colons (\:) are not treated as alignment markers. Cell-level alignment overrides the column-level alignment specified in the separator row.

Table Footers (tfoot)

You can create table footers using a row where every cell contains only === (three or more equals, with optional extra = and whitespace). This row acts as a footer divider: 

| h1  |  h2   | h3  |
| --- | :---: | --- |
| d1  |  d2   | d3  |
| d1  |  d2   | d3  |
| === |  ===  | === |
| d-4 |  d-5  | d-6 |

The === row is treated as a footer divider and is removed from the output. All following rows are rendered inside <tfoot>. The footer separator must appear after all body rows. Once the === row is encountered, all subsequent rows until the end of the table (or a blank line) are treated as footer rows.

Table Captions

Tables can have captions that appear before or after the table. Apex supports multiple caption formats:

MultiMarkdown-Style Captions

Captions in square brackets: 

[Table Caption]

| A   | B   |
| --- | --- |
| C   | D   |

Captions can appear before or after a table. They must be contiguous with the table (no other content between them), but a blank line is allowed: 

| A   | B   |
| --- | --- |
| C   | D   |

[Caption after table]

Pandoc-Style Captions

Pandoc-style [Caption lines are also supported:] 

| A   | B   |
| --- | --- |
| C   | D   |

Table: Caption after table

Pandoc-style [Caption lines are normalized to [Caption] before parsing, so they work with the same caption rendering as MultiMarkdown captions.]

Pandoc Table Attributes Extension

Apex supports Pandoc’s table_attributes extension using the : Caption syntax: 

| Key | Value |
| --- | :---: |
| one |   1   |
| two |   2   |

: Key value table {#table-id .testing key="value"}

The : Caption format (with optional IAL attributes) is recognized when it appears immediately before or after a table. IAL attributes in the caption are extracted and applied to the table element itself. Note: The : Caption syntax only works when adjacent to a table to avoid conflicts with definition list syntax. If a line starting with : is not next to a table, it will be processed as a definition list item.

Caption Position

By default, captions appear below the table. Use the --captions above option to place captions above the table instead. The --captions below option (or default) places them below. See Command Line Options for details.

Inline Attribute Lists (IALs) for Tables

Tables support Inline Attribute Lists (IALs) for adding HTML attributes like IDs, classes, and custom key-value pairs. See Inline Attribute Lists for complete IAL syntax documentation.

IALs After Tables

Tables can have IALs applied on a separate line after the table: 

| Key | Value |
| --- | :---: |
| one |   1   |
| two |   2   |

{: #data-table .striped .bordered}

This applies the attributes to the <table> element: 

<table id="data-table" class="striped bordered">
  <!-- table content -->
</table>

Apex supports both Kramdown-style IALs ({: #id .class}) and Pandoc-style IALs without the colon ({#id .class}): 

| Key | Value |
| --- | :---: |
| one |   1   |
| two |   2   |

{#table-id .my-class key="value"}

IALs in Table Captions

When using Pandoc-style captions with the : Caption syntax, IAL attributes in the caption are extracted and applied to the table: 

| Key | Value |
| --- | :---: |
| one |   1   |
| two |   2   |

: Key value table {#table-id .testing key="value"}

This is equivalent to: 

| Key | Value |
| --- | :---: |
| one |   1   |
| two |   2   |

{: #table-id .testing key="value"}

Both Kramdown-style IALs ({: #id .class}) and Pandoc-style IALs without the colon ({#id .class}) are supported in table captions.

Complete Example

Here’s a comprehensive example combining multiple advanced features: 

[Employee Performance Q4 2025]
| Department  | Employee | Q1-Q2 Average | Q3     | Q4  | Overall |
| ----------- | -------- | ------------- | ------ | --- | ------- |
| Engineering | Alice    | 93.5          | 94     | 96  | 94.25   |
| ^^          | Bob      | 89.0          | 87     | 91  | 89.00   |
| Marketing   | Charlie  | 92.0          | Absent ||| 92.00   |
| Sales       | Diana    | 87.5          | 88     | 90  | 88.50   |
| ^^          | Eve      | 93.0          | 95     | 93  | 93.50   |
| === | === | === | === | === | === |
| Total ||| :Center: ||| 92.05 |

{: .performance-table #q4-results .striped}

This example demonstrates:

  • Caption: [Employee Performance Q4 2025] before the table
  • Row spans: ^^ markers create rowspans for the Department column
  • Column spans: Consecutive pipes (| << | << |) in the “Absent” row create a colspan spanning the Q4 column
  • Per-cell alignment: :Center: in the footer row overrides column alignment
  • Table footer: === row creates a footer section
  • IAL attributes: {: .performance-table #q4-results .striped} applies classes and ID to the table
